transcription.tex: A series is a sum of a finite or infinite number of terms. In Pure Year 1, \(\Sigma\) (“capital sigma”) denotes summation.\par What we will cover:\par 1. First \(n\) integers: \(\sum_{r=1}^n r\).\par 2. First \(n\) squares: \(\sum_{r=1}^n r^2\).\par 3. First \(n\) cubes: \(\sum_{r=1}^n r^3\).\par 4. Breaking down complex sums: \(\sum_{r=1}^n(3-2r^2+4r)\).\par 5. Other bounds: \(\sum_{r=4}^{2n}r^2\).\par We will later prove some results using proof by induction.

\textbf{From History of Mathematical Notations, Vol. 2}\par 438. The sign \(\Sigma\) for summation is due to L. Euler\(^{1}\) (1755), who says, “summam indicabimus signo \(\Sigma\).” This symbol was used by Lagrange,\(^{2}\) but otherwise received little attention during the eighteenth century. A widely used notation for the sum of a series is the capital letter \(S\); it is given, for instance, in G. S. Klügel’s \(\text{W\"orterbuch.}^{3}\) The \(\Sigma\) to express “sum” occurs in 1829 in Fourier’s Theory of Heat,\(^{4}\) published in 1822, and in C. G. J. Jacobi’s\(^{5}\) elliptic functions of 1829.\par Cauchy\(^{6}\) used three indices \(m,n,r\), as in \(\sum_m^n fr\). Alfred Pringsheim\(^{7}\) marks the sum of an infinite series thus, \(\sum_0^\infty a_r\).\par Jahnke\(^{8}\) adopts in one place, as a substitute for \(\Sigma a_\nu\), the simpler sign \(\bar a\), which he borrows from geodesists, to designate the sum \(a_1+a_2+a_3+\cdots\). Additional symbols for sum are given in §410.

slides.title: Sum of Ones, Integers, Squares and Cubes

transcription.tex: These are the four essential formulae for this chapter. The last two appear in the formula booklet, but learn them too.
Sum of the first \(n\) integers: \(\sum_{r=1}^n r\)
Sum of the first \(n\) squares: \(\sum_{r=1}^n r^2\)
Sum of the first \(n\) cubes: \(\sum_{r=1}^n r^3\)
Notice:\[\sum_{r=1}^n r^3=\left(\sum_{r=1}^n r\right)^2.\]The sum of the first \(n\) cubes equals the square of the sum of the first \(n\) integers.
